learningObjective: Identify a subtle timing bug in a benchmark loop where the CPU timer records the wrong quantity because of async launch and CUDA stream ordering.

canonicalClaims.claim: A CPU timer around an async CUDA loop without synchronize measures only dispatch overhead; correct methodology synchronizes both before the start marker (to flush prior work) and before the end marker (to wait for all enqueued kernels to complete).
conditions: The workload runs asynchronously on CUDA.
The measurement target is per-iteration GPU wall time.
nonImplications: Does not imply CUDA events are unnecessary; they are an alternative or complement.
Does not imply CPU timers are unusable; wrapped with sync they are fine.

misconceptions.claim: Disabling autograd fixes async-timing measurement bugs.
misconceptions.whyWrong: no_grad does not synchronize CUDA; the timer still measures dispatch only.

misconceptions.claim: time.perf_counter has insufficient resolution for microsecond-level events.
misconceptions.whyWrong: perf_counter typically has hundreds of nanoseconds resolution on modern systems.

misconceptions.claim: Running more iterations resolves missing synchronize.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Without sync, every iteration measures dispatch alone regardless of count.

misconceptions.claim: Warmup runs synchronize as a side effect.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Warmup runs are also async; they help stabilize state but do not synchronize the subsequent timing loop.
